analysis.one_liner: Caps criminal penalties for oil and hazardous-substance spills at existing Oil Pollution Act levels.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would have limited the criminal penalties for oil and hazardous-substance spills to those in the 1990 Oil Pollution Act, died in the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee without a hearing or a vote and had no cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have made the criminal penalties in the Oil Pollution Act of 1990 the only criminal penalties that could apply to a discharge of oil or a hazardous substance under the Clean Water Act. In practice, that would bar prosecutors from using other federal criminal statutes to charge companies and individuals for spill-related conduct. It carved out conspiracy, fraud and false statements, and obstruction of justice, but everything else would be capped at the Oil Pollution Act's existing penalties. [S2] [S3]
analysis.who_benefits: Oil companies, tanker and barge operators, and other businesses that handle oil or hazardous substances would benefit, because their maximum criminal exposure for a spill would be limited to one statute's penalties. Today, the same spill can be prosecuted under several overlapping laws; the bill would have shut off those additional avenues, giving spillers certainty about the worst-case criminal penalty. [S3]

how_it_helps.text: The bill declares that the criminal penalties in sections 4301(c) and 4302 of the Oil Pollution Act of 1990 are the exclusive criminal penalties for any action connected to a discharge of oil or a hazardous substance under Clean Water Act section 311(b)(3), so prosecutors could not stack other criminal charges on top. [S3]
It preserves liability only for conspiracy, fraud and false statements, and obstruction of justice, leaving those acts punishable under general criminal law. [S2] [S3]

analysis.who_pays: Coastal communities, fisheries, and the public would bear the cost of weaker deterrence. Federal prosecutors would lose the ability to bring charges under other criminal statutes when a spill or discharge causes serious harm, meaning the legal consequence for the worst spillers would be capped at the Oil Pollution Act's penalties no matter the damage. [S3]

drawbacks.text: The strongest objection is that it would eliminate prosecutors' ability to charge serious spill conduct under other federal criminal statutes, capping punishment for even large or damaging discharges at the Oil Pollution Act's existing penalties. [S3]

The good-faith argument for it is that a single discharge can currently be prosecuted under multiple overlapping criminal laws for the same conduct, and the bill would prevent that kind of stacked punishment while still preserving charges for fraud, conspiracy, and obstruction. [S2]

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill traded real public protection for industry certainty. Companies that spill oil already face civil liability and cleanup obligations under the Oil Pollution Act; the criminal provisions of other statutes exist as a backstop for the worst conduct. Capping criminal exposure would reduce the deterrent that keeps operators careful, and the savings to industry would come at the expense of the waters, beaches, and fisheries that spills damage. Given that the bill had no cosponsors and never advanced, the Senate never seriously weighed this trade.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced on July 27, 2000 and referred to the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee, which never took it up before the 106th Congress ended on January 3, 2001.

narrative.text: Sen. John Breaux, a Louisiana Democrat, introduced the bill on July 27, 2000 and delivered introductory remarks. [S1] [S5]
The same day, the Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Environment and Public Works. [S5]
No further action was taken, and the bill died in committee when the 106th Congress ended on January 3, 2001. [S5]

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill never moved, the existing system of overlapping criminal penalties for oil and hazardous-substance discharges remained intact, which leaves prosecutors, coastal communities, and fisheries in the position they were in before. The oil and shipping industries did not get the cap on criminal exposure they would have gained from it.

for.name: Sen. John Breaux
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks on the Senate floor; it was his bill with no cosponsors.

against.name: Senate Environment and Public Works Committee
against.what_they_did: Never held a hearing, marked up, or reported the bill; it stayed in committee until the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever held and the bill drew no cosponsors from either party, so no partisan lineup on the merits is visible in the record.

industries.note: The bill would have made the Oil Pollution Act's penalties the exclusive criminal penalties for covered discharges, capping the industry's worst-case criminal exposure for a spill. The public cost is weaker criminal deterrence for the discharges that damage coastlines, fisheries, and water supplies.
Hazardous-substance discharges were covered too, so these firms would also have gained a single, fixed set of criminal penalties instead of exposure under multiple federal statutes.
